title: System submission: Kev (Qwen3.5-4B / Qwen3.5-9B), self-hostable from Hub
body:
# System submission: Kev (Qwen3.5-4B / Qwen3.5-9B), self-hostable from Hub

Hi Florian — I'd like to submit the current Kev generation to JevBench. No public endpoint on my side, so I'm asking whether you can run it on your own hardware from a public repo + Hub weights, the way you ran `kev 4B` / `kev 8B` (commit `20fa626`) in v1.2.

## System

- **Name:** Kev (research preview)
- **Setup:** Qwen3.5-4B-Base / Qwen3.5-9B-Base + LoRA + a pointer readout head, prefill-only (no generation), block-causal over shared state with isolated question branches
- **Weights:** https://huggingface.co/jaredpalmer/kev-4b and https://huggingface.co/jaredpalmer/kev-9b (adapter + `head.pt` + pinned base revision)
- **Base:** `Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B-Base` @ `1001bb4d826a52d1f399e183466143f4da7b741b`, `Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B-Base` @ `68c46c4b3498877f3ef123c856ecfde50c39f404`
- **Repro source:** https://github.com/mobailabs/kev at commit `1bcd4b7` (fork of `jaredpalmer/kev`; the native MLX / inference-worker work is under PR jaredpalmer/kev#11)

## Reproduce

```
git clone https://github.com/mobailabs/kev && cd kev
git checkout 1bcd4b7
uv sync --extra serve
KEV_DTYPE=bf16 uv run --extra serve python -m kev.serve --run jaredpalmer/kev-9b --port 8009
```

The server exposes a native TypeSafe-compatible `POST /v1/systemone`, so the existing `typesafe` adapter works unchanged (`--key-env ''`, no auth). Needs `transformers>=5.17`, `peft>=0.21`, `torch`. On CUDA the Qwen3.5 DeltaNet layers want `flash-linear-attention`; the generic PyTorch path also works (slower). On Apple Silicon it uses MLX by default.

Notes on config that you may want to name in the row:
- `KEV_DTYPE=bf16` for a GPU run (the published eval used bf16).
- Serving accepts up to 16,384 tokens for state and for state+one branch. Training used at most 384 state tokens, so long states are out of training distribution but are not truncated by the server.
- `KEV_TEMPERATURE=2.0` is the temperature fitted in-distribution for the Qwen3.5 family; default is 1.0 (uncalibrated). I'd report whichever you actually run.
- `KEV_DATE_FACTS=1` is an opt-in preprocessor that appends day-count sentences for absolute dates in the state. My hard-tier run above used it; without it temporal_numeric was 0.133 rather than 0.200. Say which you'd like measured.

## My own runs (public items, for reference only — please re-run)

I ran the public JevBench items through the local server with the official harness (`--adapter typesafe`, one request at a time). Raw `results.jsonl` / `manifest.json` / `summary.json` available on request.

| Split | n | acc |
|---|---:|---:|
| easy | 48 | 1.000 |
| original | 72 | 0.903 |
| hard (public) | 111 | 0.568 |

hard by family: adversarial 1.000, routing_hard 1.000, trap 0.875, multi_hop 0.778, ambiguous 0.571, judge_hard 0.529, tradeoff 0.500, probability 0.400, long_policy 0.368, temporal_numeric 0.200.

These were measured on an Apple M5 Max over MLX, so treat the latency as non-production and apply your usual adjustment (or ignore it — the point of the submission is Intelligence/Calibration, not my laptop's speed).

## Questions

1. Can you take this as a self-hosted submission run on your hardware, or would you rather I hand over raw results only?
2. There are already `kev 0.5B/0.6B/4B/8B` rows from commit `20fa626` (previous generation, Qwen2.5/Qwen3). Should the new Qwen3.5 checkpoints **replace** those rows or sit **alongside** them? They are different model generations.
3. Do you want me to open a PR adding a Kev adapter, or is the stock `typesafe` adapter enough?

Thanks — happy to answer anything or provide the raw artifacts.

title: [bench request]: Add metask-jev-4b (wayfind/metask-jev-4b-policy-mix, native candidate-logit readout)
body:
# [bench request]: Add metask-jev-4b (wayfind/metask-jev-4b-policy-mix, native candidate-logit readout)

Request to add **metask-jev-4b** — a Qwen3.5-4B fine-tune for typed decisions — to the ranked systems.

## What it is

A 4.54B merged model (Qwen3.5-4B @ `851bf6e` + LoRA r16, Apache-2.0) trained with the official Nimble candidate-logit objective: single forward pass, softmax over the A–Z answer-token logits, no generation. It extends the Bespoke Nimble recipe (already on the board as the 9B entry) down to 4B with two additions:

1. **View-augmented supervision** (3 criteria orderings per item, gold follows the option) — same mechanism the official pipeline uses at train time, materialized into the data.
2. **390 synthetic policy-family decisions with teacher soft labels**, mirroring the hard-tier families (long_policy, multi_hop, temporal_numeric, judge_hard, trap, probability, …), 2× upsampled.

## Serving

Single CUDA GPU (BF16) or Apple Silicon, python ≥ 3.10, ~9 GB weights. Reference inference code is in the repo; the prompt format is the official Nimble `prepare_prompts` contract, so the existing nimble adapter approach works with two config changes:

- `max_input_tokens=4096` (the model natively supports it; the 9B pipeline's 2048 limit rejects 36 of the 111 public hard items — at 4096 only 1 remains over-limit)
- per-kind temperature on the candidate logits before softmax: `choice 1.7875 / noul 2.25 / score 2.05` (fit by NLL on a held-out val split, never on eval; ECE 0.100 → 0.028)

## Our own numbers on the public items

With the prompt your harness builds, argmax over the exact label set, one request at a time, from a single RTX 4090:

| tier | items | metask-jev-4b @4096 | (at the 9B pipeline's 2048 limit) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| easy | 48 | 100.0% | 100.0% |
| judge (original) | 72 | 98.6% | 98.6% |
| hard | 111 | 59.5% | 42.3% |

We are not claiming a rank from these numbers: the held-out and imported items are yours, and speed and cost are measured from your server. The 2048-vs-4096 delta is exactly the 36 over-limit items (422 = wrong answer under your protocol); we report both so you can pick the configuration you consider comparable.

13-subset human-labeled macro (3,880 items, our eval): **79.6%** vs Bespoke Nimble-9B's published 74.8% — per-subset details in the model card.

## Hardware

One CUDA GPU with BF16 (tested on RTX 4090 24GB; weights ~9 GB, peak ~19 GB during training, inference well under). Latency p50 ~24 ms/decision on a 4090.

## Adapter PR

Ready as PR #17: https://github.com/fstandhartinger/jevbench/pull/17 — adds `jevbench/adapters/metask_jev.py`, registers it in `cli.py`, lists the model in THIRD-PARTY.md, and vendors a minimal `nimble` package (`jevbench/vendors/metask_jev/`: the official prompt builder plus a self-contained CUDA/MPS/CPU scorer), so no extra install is needed beyond the harness itself.

Zero-config verified: on a clean clone with no env set, the adapter resolves the model from the HF hub automatically and reproduces the numbers above (easy 48/48 on MPS). Env overrides: `METASK_JEV_MODEL_PATH` (local weights dir), `METASK_JEV_NIMBLE_PACKAGE` (full nimble checkout).

## Files

- Weights + full model card (13-subset table with 95% CIs, benchmark figures, honest limits): https://huggingface.co/wayfind/metask-jev-4b-policy-mix
- `install.sh` in the repo root — one-command venv + deps + model download + tokenizer-contract self-test
- Inference reference: `jev_scorer.py` / `jev_schema.py` (prompt contract + per-kind temperature, vendored from the official Nimble protocol)
- GitHub: https://github.com/metask-ai/metask-jev · internal lab: metask-ai/metask-jev-lab
- Per-decision raw results on the public items (jsonl, with probs and latency) available on request — happy to attach them here if useful.

Happy to answer questions here.

title: Add metask_jev adapter: metask-jev-4b (Qwen3.5-4B candidate-logit readout, 4096 ctx, per-kind temperature)
body:
## What this adds

An in-process adapter for [metask-jev-4b](https://huggingface.co/wayfind/metask-jev-4b-policy-mix) (Apache-2.0): a Qwen3.5-4B LoRA fine-tune trained with the official Nimble candidate-CE objective on 44.8k view-augmented public decisions + 390 policy-family soft-label decisions.

Same pattern as `laya_local`/`verdict_local`: open weights in-process, native probabilities, no HTTP. Depends on the vendored `nimble` package (bespokelabsai/nimble) on `PYTHONPATH` (`METASK_JEV_NIMBLE_PACKAGE`) and a CUDA GPU with BF16.

## Two configuration points vs the Bespoke Nimble 9B entry

1. `max_input_tokens=4096` — the base model natively supports 262,144; the 9B pipeline's 2048 limit rejects 36 of the 111 public hard items (422-scored-wrong), this model answers 88% of them correctly
2. per-kind temperature on the candidate logits before the final softmax — `choice 1.7875 / noul 2.25 / score 2.05`, fit by NLL on a held-out validation split (never on eval); ECE 0.100 → 0.028

## Self-measured on the public items

Single RTX 4090, one request at a time, argmax over the exact label set:

| tier | items | accuracy |
|---|---:|---:|
| easy | 48 | 100.0% |
| judge (original) | 72 | 98.6% |
| hard | 111 | 59.5% @4096 (42.3% @2048) |

Not claiming a rank — held-out items, Speed and Cost are yours to measure. Full tables with 95% CIs on a separate 13-subset human-labeled suite (3,880 items, macro 79.6% vs Bespoke Nimble-9B's 74.8%) in the [model card](https://huggingface.co/wayfind/metask-jev-4b-policy-mix).

## Env

- `METASK_JEV_MODEL_PATH` — local merged weights dir
- `METASK_JEV_NIMBLE_PACKAGE` — path to the vendored nimble package

Happy to adjust anything — happy to run it on a machine you can reach, too.

title: [bench request]: Add OpenJev (Loop) FP8
body:
Hey, we built [OpenJev](https://huggingface.co/openjev) at Loop. Could you add it to JevBench?

I'd suggest the [FP8 build](https://huggingface.co/openjev/openjev-FP8/tree/4ec320f267401e67c9be04d5df1be4d2b6b64f10) on one H100 80 GB. It's a fine-tuned 27B model with a native `/v1/systemone` endpoint for choice, yes/no and scoring. It returns option probabilities from one forward pass per question, up to 52 options.

The [helper and setup instructions](https://huggingface.co/openjev/openjev/blob/5ec9e5fd2f80a6fff386779b1e5ac7e389971889/README.md#quick-start) are public. The FP8 build scored 84.2% on our own 10,000-question text evaluation. I'd like to see how it does on your suite.

Weights are CC BY-NC 4.0; the helper is Apache-2.0. Happy to help with setup so you can run the full suite on your hardware.

title: [bench request]: Add local-jev (Qwen3.5-4B zero-shot, no fine-tuning; TypeSafe wire format)
body:
Request to add [local-jev](https://github.com/amithgc/local-jev) (MIT code; zero-shot `Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B`, Apache-2.0 weights, no fine-tuning and no adapter) to the ranked systems.

**What it is.** A local server that speaks TypeSafe's `/v1/systemone` wire format, so your `typesafe` adapter works unchanged (checked with the unmodified `typesafe-sdk`). The submitted model, `llm-qwen3.5-4b`, is frozen Qwen3.5-4B read at the answer token: each question and its options are laid out as one JSON object (SemIf's layout, credited), the options are lettered, and the answer is the softmax over the next-token logits of the letters. There is no generation. The state is prefilled once and its key-value cache is shared across the questions about it. Per-primitive temperatures are fitted on held-back rows of public, human-labelled datasets, never on JevBench items or on any Jev output.

```sh
git clone https://github.com/amithgc/local-jev && cd local-jev && git checkout 64a0b31
uv venv --python 3.12 .venv && uv pip install --python .venv/bin/python -e .
.venv/bin/local-jev serve --model llm-qwen3.5-4b --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8765
# first start downloads Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B (~9.3 GB) and loads the text model only (~8.5 GB, fp16 on a GPU);
# the model answers throwaway questions at load, so the first timed request is warm.
# no API key is needed; to require one, start it with LOCAL_JEV_API_KEY=<key> and pass Authorization: Bearer <key>.

python -m jevbench.cli run --tasks datasets/public/original.jsonl --adapter typesafe \
  --endpoint http://127.0.0.1:8765 --key-env '' --model llm-qwen3.5-4b ...
```

**Our own numbers on the public items** (your harness and `typesafe` adapter, one request at a time, Apple M4 Max, PyTorch on the Mac GPU):

| tier | items | llm-qwen3.5-4b |
|---|---|---|
| easy | 48 | 1.000 |
| standard (original) | 72 | 0.958 |
| hard | 111 | 0.622 |

Overall 0.805 on the 231 public items; median latency 651 ms, p95 6.9 s on that Mac. Serving has not been tested on CUDA by us, and PyTorch has no fast path for Qwen3.5's linear-attention layers on Apple GPUs, so latency on your hardware may differ a lot. We are not claiming a rank: the held-out items, calibration, speed and cost are yours to measure.

**Disclosure.** No JevBench item, paraphrase or Jev output was used for training, calibration or data generation; the model is not trained at all. The JSON-versus-plain prompt layout was chosen by measuring both on the 231 public items (plain 0.732, JSON 0.805), so the public numbers are mildly optimistic, and the held-out items may score lower.

Happy to answer questions here or rerun anything.

title: [bench request]: Add Hopper (Qwen3.5-4B + HopitAI/hopper LoRA, TypeSafe wire format)
body:
Request to add Hopper ([repository](https://github.com/hopit-ai/hopper); Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B + a LoRA adapter,
[HopitAI/hopper](https://huggingface.co/HopitAI/hopper)) to the systems you measure.

**Openness, as three facts.** Code: Apache-2.0. Weights: the adapter and its calibration map are
public on the Hugging Face Hub (and attached to the repository's GitHub release). Weight licence: Apache-2.0 for the adapter; the base model
`Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B` is Apache-2.0 (its own model card), which our licence does not change.

**What it is.** `Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B` at revision `851bf6e806efd8d0a36b00ddf55e13ccb7b8cd0a`, bf16, with
a rank-16 LoRA adapter merged in at load. One forward pass per decision, thinking off, and the
answer read as a softmax over the option letters (no generated text). A small calibration map
rescales that distribution by a temperature that depends on option count, state length,
JSON-or-not, answer type and the output's own entropy; it never changes an answer, and it was
fitted only on our own held-out data. The adapter was trained on LLM-generated decision families (labels computed in code), a
public human-labelled pool, and a JevBench-style set produced by LLM-based generation and kept only
where independent LLM solvers agreed with its answers (no JevBench item in it; see the disclosure). It serves your `/v1/systemone` wire format, so your `typesafe` adapter runs
unchanged. We are not offering an endpoint of our own.

```sh
# RunPod image runpod/pytorch:1.0.2-cu1281-torch280-ubuntu2404 (Python 3.12, CUDA 12.8.1, torch 2.8.0)
git clone https://github.com/hopit-ai/hopper && cd hopper && git checkout bad3784c314bb2a61ae98c85522970a8d2f50fd9
uv pip install --system --break-system-packages torch==2.8.0 transformers==5.17.0 peft==0.21.0 accelerate==1.15.0 flash-linear-attention==0.5.2 "https://github.com/Dao-AILab/causal-conv1d/releases/download/v1.7.0/causal_conv1d-1.7.0%2Bcu12torch2.8cxx11abiTRUE-cp312-cp312-linux_x86_64.whl"
uv pip install --system --break-system-packages --no-deps -e .
hopper-serve --adapter HopitAI/hopper --port 8080     # the calibration map ships in the package; replies carry model "hopper"
# Any CUDA GPU with 16 GB or more (bf16 weights ~9 GB, adapter merged at load). The adapter is pulled
# from the Hub on first start (public; no token needed). Start-up compiles and autotunes all Triton kernels before serving, and
# refuses to start if the fast linear-attention kernels are not active (it says what to install).
# It then warms 16 lengths between 64 and 2,048 tokens (--no-length-warmup turns that off).
# Single-threaded on purpose; no API key (any Authorization header is ignored).

python -m jevbench.cli run --tasks datasets/public/original.jsonl --adapter typesafe \
    --endpoint http://127.0.0.1:8080 --key-env '' --model hopper \
    --results RESULTS.jsonl --cost-basis self_hosted_gpu --reserve-usd 0
```

A Dockerfile and the full recipe are in the repository's README; the model card on the Hub has
the training-data sources and their licences. `POST /run` also answers `remote_inproc`'s `{"task": ...}` if you prefer that
route. We ran exactly this recipe, from the public repository at that commit with the adapter pulled from the Hub,
on a RunPod H100 NVL with the image above, using your `typesafe` adapter as the client over localhost
(our 115 public dev-half items, no network): all 115 top answers identical to our evaluation, 0 invalid
replies; standard-tier p50 / p95 39.7 / 42.7 ms in the first pass after start-up and 33.9 / 34.3 ms in a
second pass, hard-tier 44.3 / 108.6 ms; no kernel compiled during the replay; about 61 s from launch to
ready, including the Hub downloads. A pre-release copy of the same serving code gave the same answers
on an RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell (standard p50 / p95 45.6 / 46.8 ms) and, through the Docker route, on an
A10G (114 of 115; the one difference is an exact 0.5 / 0.5 tie). At these lengths the forward pass is
kernel-launch bound, so your pod's CPU matters about as much as its GPU.

**Our own numbers on the public items** (our evaluation path, argmax over the exact label set,
ties to the smallest label as in `jevbench/scoring.py`):

| tier | items | Hopper | same base, frozen, same prompt and map type |
|---|---|---|---|
| easy | 48 | 1.000 | 1.000 |
| standard (original) | 72 | 0.944 | 0.958 |
| hard | 111 | 0.685 | 0.631 |

Hard-tier top-label ECE 0.102; distribution fidelity (1 − mean total-variation distance) on the 10
public probability items 0.830. We are not claiming a rank from this: the held-out and imported
items are yours, and speed and cost are measured from your server.

**Disclosure.**
- The public items were split in half before we started. The half we developed on (115 items)
  was used as a development gate many times: 26 distinct model and prompt configurations, plus
  more than twenty calibration-map variants. Our JevBench-style training set's style sheet was
  written by reading that half, and some of its training items target behaviours we saw fail on
  its hard items. On that half the adapter scores hard 0.709.
- The other half (116) was kept as a reserve and scored only in aggregate. Our models were
  predicted on it in three earlier sessions (other configurations) and once for this system,
  chosen beforehand by a pre-registered rule. On it the adapter scores hard 0.661 (37 of 56) and
  the frozen base 0.643 (36 of 56): it is level with the frozen model on accuracy there, not ahead.
- The calibration map was fitted only on our own held-out JevBench-style items, never on a
  JevBench item.
- No JevBench item or paraphrase was used in training. Every item we wrote was checked against
  all public JevBench questions and states (normalised question identity, and any shared 8-word
  sequence) and dropped on a match; the check reads only hashes and reports only counts.
- Expect the held-out hard items to score below the public ones, and expect the judge tier, which
  we have never seen, to be the least predictable part.

Happy to answer questions here or change anything in the recipe.

title: [bench request]: Mirror (DeBERTa-v3-large, 436M) with classification probabilities and reproducible API
body:
Request to benchmark **Mirror (DeBERTa-v3-large, 436M), with a single-choice probability decoder**, on the complete frozen JevBench v1.2 set.

**Runnable public code:** https://github.com/Spico197/mirror-jevbench — submission revision `93c49aa`.

**Setup and serving:** https://github.com/Spico197/mirror-jevbench/blob/93c49aa/MIRROR-SERVING.md

**Results and evidence:** https://github.com/Spico197/mirror-jevbench/blob/93c49aa/MIRROR-API-RESULTS.md — per-item distributions, raw HTTP responses, hashes, runtime manifests and verification script are included under `results/api-v3/`.

### Model and interface

This uses the original public `Mirror_Pretrain_AllExcluded_2` weights from [Spico/Mirror](https://huggingface.co/spaces/Spico/Mirror), unchanged. The wrapper exposes `GET /health` and `POST /v1/systemone` for choice, noul and score, so your existing `typesafe` adapter works with `--key-env ''`. It can run on your own GPU; a submitter-operated endpoint is not needed for held-out questions. No benchmark request bodies are logged or sent elsewhere by the server.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Spico197/mirror-jevbench
cd mirror-jevbench
git checkout 93c49aa
python3.10 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements-mirror.txt
python scripts/setup_mirror_submission.py
python mirror_server.py --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 --device cuda
curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/health
```

Setup downloads pinned public source, tokenizer and checkpoint, and verifies the checkpoint SHA256 (`b81f6f1eed9792bf7767c1c9bd14ade382c64f120266b9eb3dc03cbafa952703`). We tested on H200 in FP32, batch size 1, TF32 off, PyTorch 2.6.0+cu124 and transformers 4.28.0. The model has 435,757,059 parameters; this is an encoder model, not a generative LLM. CPU loading is supported, but we have not measured CPU performance.

### What changed and what the probabilities mean

Mirror originally uses thresholded span decoding, which returned no classification label for 99/231 public decisions. For each candidate marker position `i`, the wrapper now computes:

```text
s_i = logsigmoid(NNW[i,i]) + logsigmoid(THW[i,i])
p_i = exp(s_i - max(s)) / sum_j exp(s_j - max(s))
```

These are the two edges required for a singleton classification span; NSW connects different span parts. Temperature is fixed at 1, with no fitted calibration. The returned choice is always the probability argmax, with lexical tie-breaking. Noul returns P(yes); ordinal questions return the full indexed distribution and expected level.

We describe these explicitly as **derived normalized classification-span scores**, not an originally trained categorical head or a claim of calibration. They are not generated/verbalized probabilities or token-generation logprobs. Your stock TypeSafe adapter labels endpoint probabilities `native`; the API and manifests carry the more precise method. Please use the provenance category appropriate to your rules.

### Public results through the unchanged TypeSafe adapter

We ran all 231 public items via actual serial HTTP using your harness revision `7ce310c7262ed49cc85853339a8a42459298e3f3` and dataset hash `dc3995d8ae1e2fc8e81ce38431add509eb8bb39b85aadfd0c7c32079382dde51`.

| Configuration | Easy | Standard/public original | Hard/public | Overall |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| **Strict 512-token context (requested submission)** | 42/48 (87.5%) | 33/72 (45.8%) | 20/111 (18.0%) | **95/231 (41.1%)** |
| Upstream truncation, diagnostic only | 42/48 (87.5%) | 33/72 (45.8%) | 41/111 (36.9%) | 116/231 (50.2%) |

The default strict configuration returns HTTP 422 for 59 inputs over 512 tokens, counting them as misses. The full length includes instruction, complete rubric, candidate labels, state and special tokens. The diagnostic mode (`--context-policy truncate`) retains the upstream state-prefix truncation behavior. Both policies were specified before this HTTP run; we are requesting the strict configuration, not selecting the higher-scoring mode.

Strict ECE is 0.2893 and multiclass Brier is 0.7256 on the 172 returned distributions; hard ECE is 0.4530 on 52 returned distributions. Rejections stay in the accuracy denominator but have no distribution for calibration. Truncation ECE is 0.2834 overall and 0.3508 on all 111 public hard items. There are no public distribution-gold items, so we have no distribution-fidelity result or official four-axis score.

The original direct-run repaired result was 117/231 (50.6%). That run supplied `task.labels` order directly. The standard TypeSafe request contains only the criteria object, so the API uses its insertion order for choice labels. We reran everything through the actual adapter and report the changed results above; we do not claim those earlier predictions as the API result.

### Timing, cost and disclosure

- Serial loopback HTTP after model load and warmup: strict p50/p95 0.0160/0.0241 s (includes fast context rejections); truncation 0.0169/0.0378 s. These are local verification measurements, not latency from your server or under production load.
- No hosted tariff exists for this wrapper; please apply your documented encoder cost-estimation policy. It does not generate output tokens, and `usage.input_tokens` reports actual encoded tokens for successful requests.
- The fix was developed after observing missing predictions on the public set. Probability normalization was proposed after seeing the repaired public accuracy. No model fine-tuning, prompt search or temperature fitting was performed on JevBench; we do not assert that original pretraining has no overlap.
- Wrapper code is Apache-2.0; upstream source and weights retain their respective licenses/terms.
- 28 focused tests passed, including choice/noul/score round trips through your HTTP adapter. All 462 rows across both runs were independently checked against raw-response hashes, recomputed scores and context handling.

Could you evaluate this pinned strict configuration on the full 534 decisions and include it with the probability-conversion and context-limit disclosures? The public code and weights can run entirely on your hardware.

title: [bench request]: Add NInfer (Qwen3.8-27B NVFP4 and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, native option-logit readout; adapter and TypeSafe shim included)
body:
Please consider two systems served by [NInfer](https://github.com/igorls/ninfer), a from-scratch
C++/CUDA inference engine for NVIDIA Blackwell (`sm_120a`), qualified on Windows and buildable on
Linux. Nothing is trained or fitted to the benchmark: the engine exposes the model's own next-token
distribution over the option letters through its `logprob_candidates` extension, so each decision is
one forward pass and no text is generated. Both use public Qwen weights in NInfer's native `.ninfer`
format:

| system | weights | resident VRAM | recommended GPU |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ninfer-qwen3.8-27b` | [neroued/Qwen3.8-27B-nvfp4-NInfer](https://huggingface.co/neroued/Qwen3.8-27B-nvfp4-NInfer) (NVFP4, 20 GiB, from Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B via unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4) | ~24 GB at the profile below | any Blackwell card with 32 GB: RTX 5090, RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell (your RunPod card) |
| `ninfer-qwen3.8-flash-next` | [igorls/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-mixed-NInfer](https://huggingface.co/igorls/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-mixed-NInfer) (NVFP4 experts + FP8 projections + INT4 PLE, 105 GiB on disk; 125B total, 6B active, plus a 51B n-gram embedding and a 4B MTP) | ~80 GB at the profile below | RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell 96 GB (RunPod has it) |

**Configuration** (fork commit `3d6abdf8`, branch `research/qwen4-flash-next`; the engine sources are
those of `a77d4ed5`, which is the build measured below, plus one fix to the shim script):

```sh
git clone https://github.com/igorls/ninfer && cd ninfer && git checkout 3d6abdf8
# Linux: CUDA 13.1+, CMake 3.28+, Ninja; text-only build is enough
cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DNINFER_BUILD_MEDIA=OFF
cmake --build build -j
# or: docker build -t ninfer .   (the Dockerfile in the repo root builds the same two binaries)

hf download neroued/Qwen3.8-27B-nvfp4-NInfer qwen3_8_27b_nvfp4.ninfer --local-dir models
./build/apps/ninfer-serve models/qwen3_8_27b_nvfp4.ninfer --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8010 \
  --model-id qwen3.8-27b --max-context 8192 --kv-capacity 8192 --max-concurrency 1 \
  --kv-dtype fp8 --desktop-reserve-gib 1

hf download igorls/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-mixed-NInfer qwen3_8_flash_next_mixed.ninfer --local-dir models
./build/apps/ninfer-serve models/qwen3_8_flash_next_mixed.ninfer --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8010 \
  --model-id qwen3.8-flash-next --max-context 32768 --kv-capacity 65536 --max-concurrency 2 \
  --prefill-chunk 8192 --kv-dtype fp8 --gdn-state-dtype bf16 --spec mtp --draft-tokens 4 \
  --desktop-reserve-gib 1
```

Wait for `server status=ready`; Flash-Next materializes 76 GB of weights and warms a host-side
embedding table, so send one warm-up request before timing. The first request after start is
slower on both.

**Two ways to ask it.** `tools/bench/jevbench/ninfer_native.py` is an adapter in your adapter
contract (one Chat Completions request per decision; happy to open it as a pull request). Or run
`tools/bench/jevbench/typesafe_shim.py --ninfer http://127.0.0.1:8010/v1 --ninfer-model qwen3.8-27b
--port 8000`, which serves `POST /v1/systemone` so your `typesafe` adapter runs unchanged with
`--endpoint http://127.0.0.1:8000 --key-env ''`. Both build the identical prompt: the state, the
instructions and the options as `A. label: description` lines, thinking off, one greedy token, and
the distribution read from the option-letter logits and renormalised over the letters. The
requested model name selects the readout: `ninfer-qwen3.8-27b` is the raw distribution,
`ninfer-qwen3.8-27b-t1.5` divides the option logits by 1.5 before the softmax (calibration only,
argmax unchanged). We ask for both 27B rows, see the disclosure.

**Our numbers on the 231 public items** (one request at a time, argmax over the exact label set,
failures count as wrong, none occurred; the score column uses your v1.2 formula on the tiers we can
see, with the judge tier's weight renormalised away). All rows are the Linux build of commit
`a77d4ed5` from the Dockerfile above, run natively under WSL2 Ubuntu 24.04 on an RTX PRO 6000
Blackwell with the exact serve commands above (Flash-Next's Windows build of the same commit gave
the identical answers and probabilities):

| system | easy 48 | standard 72 | hard 111 | hard ECE | fidelity (1 − TVD, 10 items) | p50 / p95 standard | score (see cost) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ninfer-qwen3.8-27b | 1.000 | 0.972 | 0.667 | 0.134 | 0.662 | 0.033 s / 0.055 s | 71.0 at $0.09, 66.6 at $0.20 |
| ninfer-qwen3.8-27b-t1.5 | 1.000 | 0.972 | 0.667 | 0.091 | 0.693 | same | 72.4 at $0.09, 68.0 at $0.20 |
| ninfer-qwen3.8-flash-next | 1.000 | 0.986 | 0.793 | 0.096 | 0.826 | 0.094 s / 0.120 s | 71.5 at $0.15 |
| Jev 1.13.0, your per-task file, same items | 1.000 | 0.986 | 0.730 | | | | |

Latencies are localhost wall time on our box; yours will include the network path. Two cost bases
because we do not know which you will apply: your SimpleJev Qwen3.8-27B row used a $0.09 per million
size-class reference, and OpenRouter now lists `qwen/qwen3.8-27b` itself at $0.20 per million input
tokens (there is also a `:free` listing, which we understand you do not price as free).
`qwen/qwen3.8-flash` is $0.15 per million input tokens at its only provider, Alibaba Cloud. Every
decision reads about 685 input tokens and generates nothing.

**Disclosure.**

- Nothing was trained. The prompt wording was fixed before the first run and never changed.
- The temperature of 1.5 for the 27B was chosen on these public hard items after the raw run, by
  sweeping 0.7 to 4 and reading ECE and fidelity, so treat its calibration as a development-set
  number. We declare it here before your run rather than applying it afterwards, and we ask for the
  raw row beside it. For Flash-Next the same sweep found 1.0 already optimal, so it has one row.
- Option order. Our adapter presents choice options in the dataset's `labels` order; TypeSafe's
  wire format carries the criteria object, which your files store in key order, and 119 of the 139
  public choice items differ between the two. Through the shim (wire order) Flash-Next scores hard
  0.775 instead of 0.793, ECE 0.089, fidelity 0.750, with 11 argmax flips, all near 0.5. If you
  run through the shim, expect that variant.
- Numerics. Read-only one-shot requests take a single prefill pass in this commit (publishing
  chat requests keep the split at turn boundaries). The option logits on borderline hard items
  move with execution decomposition and build at the few-percent level: the Windows build of the
  same commit answered 78 of the 111 public hard items where the Linux build answered 74, with six
  argmax flips between them and identical probabilities on most items. Expect the held-out hard
  items to come in below the public numbers, as everyone else's have.
- The public items were consulted repeatedly during development; the held-out ones are yours.

If anything here is unclear or something does not build on your side, ask.

title: New submission: smalljev semantic-v9 (Apache-2.0, 2.5B, JevBench 65.53 on v1.2 / Intelligence 62.19)
body:
## smalljev semantic-v9 — JevBench submission

### System
- **Name:** smalljev semantic-v9
- **Author:** isHeSatoshi (Am I Satoshi)
- **License:** Apache-2.0 (code + weights)
- **Backbone:** `openbmb/MiniCPM5-2B-Base` (Apache-2.0)
- **Variant:** 2.5B dense + LoRA + OptionScorerHead + BinaryNoulHead + OrdinalScoreHead
- **Probability origin:** native (option-span mean-pool + shared head softmax; no `generate()`, zero generated tokens per request)

### Score measured
- **JevBench Score: 65.53 / 100** on JevBench v1.2 (4-axis geometric composite, 231 of 534 public items)
  - Intelligence: **62.19** (easy 97.92 / standard 69.44 / hard 38.74; judge tier not in upstream public repo)
  - Calibration: 63.19 (Brier 0.522, ECE 0.157, mean TVD 0.423)
  - Speed: 79.67 (p50 175 ms, p95 1.00 s, adjusted ×2 +0.15 s for self-hosted)
  - Cost: 58.90 (estimated $0.0234 / 1k decisions at $0.04/M-input reference)
- measured on a 16 GB consumer GPU (RTX 4060 Ti), ~70 s wall time for all 231 items

### Artifacts
- **Repo:** https://github.com/isHeSatoshi/smalljev
- **Adapter file:** `jevbench_eval/adapter/smalljev_semantic_adapter.py` (lives in the dev branch, not in the public repo)
- **Weights (HF Hub):** https://huggingface.co/isHeSatoshi/smalljev-semantic-v9
  - `semantic-v9-lora/adapter_config.json` + `adapter_model.safetensors` (17.2 MB)
  - `semantic-v9-scorer.pt`
  - `semantic-v9-noulscore.pt`

### How to run
```bash
# install the public library + bench extras
git clone https://github.com/isHeSatoshi/smalljev
cd smalljev
pip install -e ".[bench]"

# grab the weights from HF Hub
huggingface-cli download openbmb/MiniCPM5-2B-Base --local-dir ./weights/base
huggingface-cli download isHeSatoshi/smalljev-semantic-v9 --local-dir ./weights/semantic-v9

# the actual JevBench harness lives on the v9 development branch (not the public slim repo)
git checkout v9-dev
python jevbench_eval/scripts/run_v12.py \
    --variant-label  smalljev_semantic_v9 \
    --adapter-dir    ./weights/semantic-v9/semantic-v9-lora \
    --scorer-ckpt    ./weights/semantic-v9/semantic-v9-scorer.pt \
    --noulscore-ckpt ./weights/semantic-v9/semantic-v9-noulscore.pt \
    --harness-root   ./jevbench_upstream \
    --run-dir        ./runs/2026-09-21_semantic_v9_v12 \
    --tiers          easy,standard,hard
python jevbench_eval/scripts/summarize_v12.py \
    --run-dir      ./runs/2026-09-21_semantic_v9_v12 \
    --harness-root ./jevbench_upstream
# → JevBench Score (4-axis geometric): 65.53
```

Pinned environment: torch 2.8.0+cu129, transformers 4.57.6, peft 0.15.2.

### Caveats
- 231 / 534 items on v1.2 (the 303 held-out, easy-heldout, judge, router items aren't in the upstream public repo). v1.2.7 has all 534 items including judge (146); pulling the third-party auto-model-router data via `scripts/import_router.py` would unlock a 299-item public run.
- Cost basis is estimated against OpenRouter `Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct` $0.04/M-input × measured input tokens (same estimator the public leaderboard uses for self-hosted systems).
- No benchmark-specific calibration was fit on JevBench. No temperature scaling, no vector scaling, no isotonic fit. Just the raw model.
- Live workspace integrity was preserved during measurement (`git status --short` identical before and after).

Smallest model in the published ranked set; fits in ~5 GB VRAM; the only one whose probability origin is span-pooled native softmax rather than letter-position softmax.

Happy to provide anything else — adapter revisions, additional variants, alternate run scripts. Thanks for maintaining JevBench.

- Base Architecture: Pure geometric complex polynomial escape-time dynamics (Mandelbrot boundary phase resonance)
- Weights / Parameters: **0 Bytes** (deterministic mathematical seed, 0 Bytes VRAM, 0 MB GPU RAM)

---

### What it is
A zero-memory machine-native System-One decision engine designed for instant, typed discrete judgments (`noul`, `choice`, `score`).

```sh
git clone https://github.com/pCwOrM/werr.git && cd werr
python -m werr.server --port 8443
```

title: [bench request]: jqv serving code is now public (Octalab-Inc/jqv) — re-run for a rankable row
body:
Follow-up to #6 (jqv, partial row in v1.2.7): the serving code is now public, so I would like to request a re-run that can include the held-out hard items on your own hardware, making the row rankable.

**Repository.** https://github.com/Octalab-Inc/jqv — commit `0189b67`. Weights are the public `Qwen/Qwen3-32B` (Apache-2.0, BF16, no fine-tuning). Run instructions written for you: [`docs/jevbench-serving.md`](https://github.com/Octalab-Inc/jqv/blob/0189b67/docs/jevbench-serving.md).

**Configuration.** Identical to the one you measured in #6: `packed` engine (state prefilled once, each question an isolated branch behind a block attention mask, answer read from the option-letter logits in one forward pass, no decoding), one scalar temperature 3.0225814579771493 fitted on 400 MMLU validation items and stored with provenance in the repo (`results/mmlu_packed_qwen3-32b_temperature.json`), served over TypeSafe's wire format (`POST /v1/systemone`), so the `typesafe` adapter runs unchanged with `--key-env ''`. `GET /health` reports `prompt_hash` `4f85a0b34776` and the temperature, which lets you confirm the configuration matches #6 before the run.

```sh
git clone https://github.com/Octalab-Inc/jqv && cd jqv && uv sync
JQV_MODEL=Qwen/Qwen3-32B JQV_ENGINE=packed JQV_TEMPERATURE_FILE=results/mmlu_packed_qwen3-32b_temperature.json \
uv run uvicorn jqv.server:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000
curl -s localhost:8000/health   # model, engine, prompt_hash 4f85a0b34776, calibration.temperature 3.0225814579771493
```

**Hardware.** About 65 GB of memory for the BF16 weights. We ran it on an Apple M5 Max through PyTorch/MPS; on CUDA it should work unchanged (`JQV_DEVICE=cuda`) but we have not run it there. If the masked-attention path gives trouble on your stack, `JQV_ENGINE=kvcache` or `JQV_ENGINE=naive` produce the same choice logits (checked by the equivalence tests in the repo).

**Expected numbers.** On the public tiers the configuration reproduced our own numbers exactly in #6 (easy 1.000, standard 0.958, hard 0.622, hard-tier top-label ECE 0.107), so a healthy run on your side should show the same public-tier figures before the held-out items.

**Cost basis.** Whatever you apply to open weights you run yourselves; the OpenRouter `qwen/qwen3-32b` input tariff you used in #6 is fine with me.

**Disclosure.** Unchanged from #6: no benchmark item was used for training; the only fitted quantity is the temperature (MMLU validation); the public 231 items were used once as a development gate when choosing this configuration over an option-order-averaged variant.

Thank you for the v1.2.7 run and for documenting the endpoint condition; happy to answer questions here.

title: [bench request]: Add decision-machine-1 (milliseconds.ai, TypeSafe wire format, production API)
body:
Request to add **decision-machine-1** to the ranked systems. 

It is the decisions API at `https://api.milliseconds.ai`, run by [milliseconds.ai](https://www.milliseconds.ai). It is a production API with a public pricing.

### What it is
A multimodal decision model behind a typed API: yes/no, label, rating, answer span, JSON Schema fill, entities, value check. No chat, no free generation. Weights are not published.

### Wire format
On top of the standard Milliseconds API (adapted to our specific use cases), it serves TypeSafe's `POST /v1/systemone`, so your `typesafe` adapter applies unchanged. `noul` returns `noul`; `choice` returns `choice` and `probabilities` keyed by option name; `score` returns `score`, `legend` and `probabilities` keyed by level index. Docs: https://docs.milliseconds.ai/typesafe/overview

```sh
python -m jevbench.cli run --tasks datasets/public/original.jsonl \
  --adapter typesafe --endpoint https://api.milliseconds.ai --key-env MS_API_KEY \
  --model decision-machine-1 --price-in-per-m 0.04 --price-out-per-m 0 --delay-s 2.2 \
  --results RUN/results.jsonl --raw-dir RUN/raw --ledger RUN/ledger.jsonl --cap-usd 5
```

#### Differences from TypeSafe: 

- `model` must be `decision-machine-1`; validation errors are `400`, not `422`; 
- `choice` takes 2 to 64 options, `score` 2 to 10 levels, `state` at most 20,000 characters

### Key and rate limit
You can sign up for a free key at https://console.milliseconds.ai/signup 

Test keys allow 30 requests per minute, and JevBench harness stops on the first 429, so I'd recommend keeping `--delay-s 2.2`. 
A full 534-decision run takes about 25 minutes and well under one million tokens, against 125 million free per month.

I'm also super happy to hand out free tokens, and give access to a higher tier. If you'd like, email bap@cloudraker.com and I'll get your account upgraded! 

The inference infrastructure is identical between free and prod key, but rate limits change.

### Bench run on our side
Below are our own numbers on the public items, one request at a time, argmax over the exact label set.

| tier | items | accuracy | how measured |
|---|---|---|---|
| standard (original) | 72 | 0.750 | your `typesafe` adapter against `/v1/systemone`, 2026-09-20, 0 failed |
| easy | 48 | 1.000 | our adapter against the native routes, same mapping, 2026-09-20 |
| hard (public) | 111 | 0.505 | same run as easy |

Hard-tier top-label ECE on the public items is 0.13. Standard-tier p50 through `/v1/systemone` was 0.17 s and p95 0.31 s from Montréal, network included.

### Speed and cost basis
Production API served from the region nearest the caller; a request from Germany lands in the European region (we have 3 inference regions for now: wnam, enam, weur). 

Public pricing: $0.04 per million input tokens, output free (https://docs.milliseconds.ai/reference/pricing). 

Every response reports the billed input in `usage.input_tokens` and the `x-input-tokens` header. 
On our public-item runs that came to about $0.034 per 1,000 decisions.

### Openness
Proprietary API, closed weights, no self-hosting option.

Thanks for the hard work!

title: [bench request]: Add jqv (Qwen3-32B zero-shot, TypeSafe wire format, public endpoint)
body:
Request to add **jqv** (Qwen3-32B, Apache-2.0 base weights, no fine-tuning; TypeSafe wire format) to the ranked systems, via a public endpoint.

**What it is.** An open reconstruction of the Jev inference design on a stock decoder LLM: the state is prefilled once, every question runs as an isolated branch (block attention mask, no cross-question leakage), and the answer is read directly from the option-letter logits in one forward pass (no decoding). The served probabilities are temperature-scaled with a single scalar (T = 3.02) fitted on 400 MMLU validation items; provenance is reported by `GET /health`. The submitted configuration is the zero-shot backbone without any decision training. It serves TypeSafe's wire format (`POST /v1/systemone`, choice / noul / score, string or JSON state), so your `typesafe` adapter works unchanged.

**Endpoint (self-hosted, no billing).**

- `https://asn-front-mix-develop.trycloudflare.com` — a Cloudflare Quick Tunnel to an Apple M5 Max (128 GB) in Japan running Qwen3-32B in BF16 on PyTorch/MPS, one request at a time.
- No API key: run with `--key-env ''`; any `model` value is accepted and echoed back (we use `jqv-qwen3-32b`).
- Cost basis: `no_billable_account_public_endpoint`.
- Please send one warm-up request before timing. Raw latency on the machine is p50 0.65 s on the public standard tier; your wall time will include the network path from Germany to Japan.
- The tunnel stays up until your run is done — please comment here when finished so I can take it down. The source is not public yet; I can share it on request.

```sh
python -m jevbench.cli run --tasks datasets/public/original.jsonl \
  --adapter typesafe --endpoint https://asn-front-mix-develop.trycloudflare.com --key-env '' --model jqv-qwen3-32b \
  --cost-basis no_billable_account_public_endpoint --reserve-usd 0 --delay-s 0.2 ...
```

**Our own numbers on the public items** (your harness at commit 7ce310c, `typesafe` adapter, one request at a time, argmax over the exact label set, served probabilities as above):

| tier | items | jqv (Qwen3-32B, zero-shot) |
|---|---|---|
| easy | 48 | 1.000 |
| standard (original) | 72 | 0.958 |
| hard | 111 | 0.622 |

Hard-tier top-label ECE 0.107 (raw p50 0.65 s). No distribution-gold items are public, so we have no distribution-fidelity number. We are not claiming a rank from this: the held-out and judge items are yours, and speed is measured from your server.

**Disclosure.** No training was done on any benchmark item; the only fitted quantity is the temperature (MMLU validation). The public 231 items were used to evaluate nine configurations (three backbone sizes × zero-shot / option-order averaging / LoRA head), and the choice to submit the zero-shot 32B configuration rather than the option-averaged one was made after seeing those public-tier numbers, so treat the public tiers as a development gate once. JSON-state items are rendered to the model as pretty-printed JSON text.

title: [bench request]: Add reflex-27b (Qwen3.8-27B through reflex, frozen, two option orders; TypeSafe wire format)
body:
A second reflex entry, please, alongside the pending `reflex` (4B) request in #3: the same open re-creation of the Jev design ([kshetrajna12/reflex](https://github.com/kshetrajna12/reflex), MIT) running the frozen **Qwen3.8-27B** (Apache-2.0) with no adapter, no calibration file, and each question read in two distinct option orders and averaged.

**What it is.** The state is encoded once and cached; every question runs as an isolated branch in one forward pass; the answer distribution is read from the option-label logits, no decoding. For each choice/score question the options are presented in two distinct orders (yes/no questions both ways round) inside the same pass and the two distributions are averaged. No weights are trained and nothing is fitted: temperature 1. It serves TypeSafe's wire format, so your `typesafe` adapter runs unchanged.

Configuration (commit `b77f03b`, branch `main`):

```sh
git clone https://github.com/kshetrajna12/reflex && cd reflex && git checkout b77f03b
uv sync
REFLEX_API_KEY=any uv run reflex-serve --model Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B --permutations 2 \
    --served-name reflex-27b --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000
# bf16, ~54 GB of weights: an 80 GB GPU (A100/H100) or a 64 GB+ unified-memory box.
# The first request compiles Triton kernels (~20 s); send one warm-up request before timing.
```

The 4B entry in #3 is unchanged except that it too now reads two orders (`git checkout stable`, `reflex-serve --stable`); happy to have that picked up in the same round or left as filed.

**Our own numbers on the public items** (your adapter's requests, one at a time, argmax over the exact label set; served on a DGX Spark GB10):

| tier | items | reflex-27b | reflex (4B, 2 orders) |
|---|---|---|---|
| easy | 48 | 1.000 | 1.000 |
| standard (original) | 72 | 0.958 | 0.917 |
| hard | 111 | 0.766 | 0.685 |

Hard-tier top-label ECE 0.061, distribution fidelity on the 10 public probability items 0.827; p50 latency 0.6 s on easy/standard items and 1.0 s on hard ones on our box. We are not claiming a rank from this: the held-out and imported items are yours, and speed and cost are measured from your server.

**Disclosure.** No training and no benchmark item or paraphrase is involved in this configuration. The prompt wording and the two-order readout were selected on our own external sets (support intents, MNLI-mismatched, toxic-chat, Yelp; details in the repo's `docs/results/order-averaging.md`) and then checked on the public 231, which we have consulted repeatedly during development, so treat the public numbers as development-suite numbers and expect the held-out hard items to come in below them. Full method and every negative result are in the repo.

If a 60 GB GPU is an obstacle for the run, say so and we can host the endpoint for you for the duration.

title: [bench request]: Add decider-35b-a3b (Mapika/decider-35b-a3b, TypeSafe wire format)
body:
Request to add [decider-35b-a3b](https://huggingface.co/Mapika/decider-35b-a3b) (Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-Base, 34.7B parameters with 3B active per token, Apache-2.0 weights and code) to the ranked systems. It is the larger sibling of decider-2b (#2); both serve the same wire format, so one adapter covers both.

**What it is.** A one-pass decision model: the letter logits at an answer slot are read for every option, no decoding. The supervised recipe of decider-2b (one epoch of cross-entropy on the slot readout over about 95 public decision datasets and Jev's input shapes) applied to the 35B mixture-of-experts base with the routed experts frozen and the Muon optimizer; no RL stage. Every question is scored in its own row, so option order and the other questions do not change an answer. Code and recipe: https://github.com/Mapika/decider (`moe/`, `docs/HISTORY.md`).

It serves TypeSafe's `POST /v1/systemone`, so your `typesafe` adapter applies unchanged:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/Mapika/decider && cd decider
uv venv --python 3.12 .venv312 && uv pip install -p .venv312/bin/python -e ".[serve]"
scripts/serve.sh Mapika/decider-35b-a3b 8000      # one CUDA GPU with 80 GB or more, bf16, 65 GB of weights; downloads on first use
                                                  # transformers>=5.17 and torch>=2.14 (grouped-GEMM experts), flash-linear-attention

python -m jevbench.cli run --tasks datasets/public/original.jsonl \
  --adapter typesafe --endpoint http://127.0.0.1:8000 --key-env '' --model decider-35b-a3b \
  --cost-basis self_hosted_gpu --reserve-usd 0 ...
```

`noul` returns `noul`, `choice` and `score` return `probabilities` keyed by option name and level index, as in your adapter's mapping. An NVFP4 build for vLLM and TensorRT-LLM on Blackwell is at [decider-35b-a3b-nvfp4](https://huggingface.co/Mapika/decider-35b-a3b-nvfp4) (19.6 GB; 1.0 to 1.5 accuracy points under bf16 on our fixtures); its card has the readout through vLLM, but the HTTP server above runs the bf16 weights.

**Our own numbers on the public items**, with the request your adapter builds, argmax over the exact label set, one request at a time:

| tier | items | decider-35b-a3b v1 | decider-2b v10 |
|---|---|---|---|
| easy | 48 | 1.000 | 1.000 |
| standard (original) | 72 | 0.972 | 0.847 |
| hard | 111 | 0.676 | 0.459 |

Hard-tier top-label ECE is 0.15. The remaining hard misses are temporal-numeric items (5 of 15 correct), long-policy and judge-hard items; adversarial, trap and hard-routing items are all correct. Standard-tier misses are one adequacy and one policy item.

**Speed and cost basis.** One NVIDIA B300, eager PyTorch (the CUDA-graph engine of the package is not yet enabled for this architecture): 47 ms per request with three questions on a 90-token state, about 520 decisions per second in batches of 64. decider-2b on the same machine serves at 4 ms per request. If you rank one of the two, this is the stronger entry; the 2B is the cheaper one.

title: [bench request]: Add reflex (kshetrajna12/reflex-qwen3.5-4b-lora, TypeSafe wire format)
body:
Request to add [reflex](https://github.com/kshetrajna12/reflex) (Qwen3.5-4B + a LoRA adapter,
[kshetrajna12/reflex-qwen3.5-4b-lora](https://huggingface.co/kshetrajna12/reflex-qwen3.5-4b-lora);
MIT code and adapter, Apache-2.0 base weights) to the ranked systems.

**What it is.** An open re-creation of the Jev design: the state is encoded once and cached,
every question runs as an isolated branch in one pass, and the answer is read directly from the
label logits (no decoding). Trained with a proper scoring rule on public datasets and synthetic
correct-by-construction data ("RLCD-lite"); temperatures fitted per primitive on our own held-out
set. It serves TypeSafe's wire format, so your `typesafe` adapter works unchanged.

```sh
git clone https://github.com/kshetrajna12/reflex && cd reflex && git checkout 1add693
uv sync
REFLEX_API_KEY=any uv run reflex-serve --model Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B \
    --adapter kshetrajna12/reflex-qwen3.5-4b-lora --served-name reflex --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000
# adapter + calibration.json are pulled from the Hub; ~9 GB bf16, any 16 GB CUDA GPU;
# the first request compiles Triton kernels (~20 s), so send one warm-up request before timing.

export REFLEX_KEY=any
python -m jevbench.cli run --tasks datasets/public/original.jsonl \
  --adapter typesafe --endpoint http://127.0.0.1:8000 --key-env REFLEX_KEY --model reflex \
  --cost-basis self_hosted_gpu --reserve-usd 0 ...
```
A Dockerfile (`docker/Dockerfile`) and the full recipe are in `docs/SERVING.md`.

**Our own numbers on the public items** (your adapter's requests, one at a time, argmax over the
exact label set):

| tier | items | reflex |
|---|---|---|
| easy | 48 | 1.000 |
| standard (original) | 72 | 0.944 |
| hard | 111 | 0.604 |

Hard-tier top-label ECE 0.117; distribution fidelity on the 10 public probability items 0.689.
We are not claiming a rank from this: the held-out and imported items are yours, and speed and
cost are measured from your server.

**Disclosure.** The training recipes were designed after looking at which public families the
raw model failed (answer adequacy, rule-based routing, base-rate probabilities; a long-policy
recipe exists in the repo but this adapter was not trained on it). No benchmark item or paraphrase was used in training; `reflex-data check-overlap` refuses to
train if any training row shares an 8-word sequence with a public item. The public 231 were used
as a development gate four times (three adapters, one re-calibration), so expect the held-out hard items to score somewhat below the
public ones.

Happy to answer questions here or rerun anything.

title: [bench request]: Add decider-2b (Mapika/decider-2b, TypeSafe wire format)
body:
Request to add [decider-2b](https://huggingface.co/Mapika/decider-2b) (Qwen3.5-2B-Base, 1.9B parameters, Apache-2.0 weights and code) to the ranked systems.

**What it is.** A one-pass decision model: the letter logits at an answer slot are read for every option, no decoding. It serves TypeSafe's wire format, so your `typesafe` adapter works unchanged:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/Mapika/decider && cd decider
uv venv --python 3.12 .venv312 && uv pip install -p .venv312/bin/python -e ".[serve]"
scripts/serve.sh Mapika/decider-2b 8000          # one CUDA GPU, bf16, about 4 GB; downloads the weights on first use

python -m jevbench.cli run --tasks datasets/public/original.jsonl \
  --adapter typesafe --endpoint http://127.0.0.1:8000 --key-env '' --model decider-2b \
  --cost-basis self_hosted_gpu --reserve-usd 0 ...
```

`noul` returns `noul`, `choice` and `score` return `probabilities` keyed by option name and level index, as in your adapter's mapping. Every question is scored in its own row, so option order and the other questions do not change an answer. The current weights are v10 (v8 continued with outcome-reward RL on live MiniWoB++ click tasks and exact games; details in the repository's `docs/RL.md`). The previous weights are under the Hub tag `v8`.

**Our own numbers on the public items**, with the request your adapter builds, argmax over the exact label set, one request at a time:

| tier | items | decider-2b v10 | decider-2b v8 |
|---|---|---|---|
| easy | 48 | 1.000 | 1.000 |
| standard (original) | 72 | 0.847 | 0.861 |
| hard | 111 | 0.459 | 0.459 |

Hard-tier top-label ECE is 0.30. On the standard tier the misses are answer-adequacy judgments and routing; on the hard tier the long-policy, multi-hop and temporal-numeric families. We are not claiming a rank from this: the held-out and imported items are yours, and speed and cost are measured from your server. Median latency on our GPU was 10 ms per decision, without the compiled engine; `DECIDER_COMPILE=1` (the default in `scripts/serve.sh`) is faster after warm-up.

If a self-hosted run is an option on your side, the command above is all it needs. Happy to answer questions here.
